L61: 
L62: Let $x\in[0,1]^{3\times H\times W}$ be an image and $M\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W}$ be a binary mask defining the attack region. For global attacks, $M$ is an all-ones matrix; for patch attacks, $M$ is 1 only within a fixed region and 0 elsewhere. The perturbed image is defined as:
L63: 
L64:  | $$x_{\delta}=\Pi_{[0,1]}(x+M\odot\delta),\qquad\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon,$$  |  | (1)
L65: where $\odot$ denotes the element-wise Hadamard product and $\Pi$ clips to the valid pixel range. We attack a surrogate ensemble $\mathcal{E}=\{f_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J}$ of open-source MLLMs. Each model receives $x_{\delta}$ and a fixed text prompt $t$ through its preprocessing pipeline $\Phi_{j}$. For model $f_{j}$, let $z_{j}$ denote its next-token logits at the final prompt position $\tau_{j}$.
L66: We compute top-$k$ probabilities $p_{j}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{j}^{(k)}/T_{e})$, where $z_{j}^{(k)}$ retains the top $k$ logits and $T_{e}$ is the temperature, and maximize the Shannon entropy $H(p_{j})=-\sum_{v}p_{j}(v)\log p_{j}(v)$. The attack maximizes entropy averaged across models:
L67:  | $$\max_{\|\delta\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon}\;\frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}H\big(p_{j}(x_{\delta},t)\big).$$  |  | (2)
L68: 
L69: We perform projected gradient ascent (PGD) [cite15†1 ], optionally masking the gradient to constrain updates to the patch area:
L70: 
L71:  | $$\delta\leftarrow\Pi_{\|\cdot\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon}\left(\delta+\eta(M\odot\nabla_{\delta}\mathcal{L})\right),$$  |  | (3)
L72: 
L73: with $\mathcal{L}$ equal to the negative of the entropy objective.

L83: ## 3 Experiments
L84: Setup. The base image is a screenshot of the CCRU homepage that is resized to $448\times 448$ to reduce training time. We also tested other websites and observed no substantial differences in results. For the Adversarial CAPTCHA experiments, we use the full $1024\times 576$ webpage screenshot and optimize a fixed $224\times 224$ region at its center.
L85: In all scenarios, we optimize the perturbation $\delta$ for 50 iterations and select the final adversarial example by choosing the one that yields the highest averaged entropy across the training ensemble. We used four open-source models: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen3-VL-2B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and LLaVA-1.6-7B.
L86: Metrics & Baselines. We report the Shannon entropy of the next-token distribution, restricted to the top $k=50$ logits. We found that aggressive truncation (e.g., $k=5$) reduces transferability, while full-vocabulary optimization introduces training instability. This restriction also standardizes entropy values across models with different vocabulary sizes. We evaluate black-box transfer using a cross-family held-out protocol.
L87: Specifically, we optimize on two models from one family and evaluate on a held-out model from a different family. We compare the adversarial output against two baselines: the clean, unperturbed screenshot and an image perturbed with uniform random noise $\delta_{uni}\sim\mathcal{U}(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$.
L88: Across all models, entropy for the clean image remains low (below 0.6) and comparable to the random noise baseline; a modest entropy increase ($\sim$0.2) was observed for Qwen3-VL under the unconstrained budget noise. We report the Effective Confusion Ratio (ECR), which quantifies how much the attack outperforms both the clean image and the random noise baseline:
L89:  | $$\mathrm{ECR}=\frac{H(f(x_{\mathrm{adv}}))}{\max\big[H(f(x_{\mathrm{clean}})),\,H(f(x_{\mathrm{noise}}))\big]}$$  |  | (4)
L90: 
L91: Values above 1 indicate that the adversarial example induces higher uncertainty than both clean and random-noise baselines.
L92: Proprietary Evaluation. For proprietary models, we evaluate transfer using the LMSYS Arena platform^{1}^{1} 1 https://lmarena.ai with the prompt “Describe this image.” and the adversarial image as input. We count an attack as successful when the model’s description is clearly unrelated to the actual image content.

L201: ## Study 4: Safety alignment strategies show limited effectiveness and potentially adverse effects on LLMs’ complicit behaviors
L202: To analyze the impact of current mainstream safety alignment methods and datasets on LLMs’ complicit behaviors, we employ two widely adopted alignment methods, SFT and DPO (cite38†Wei et al., 2021 ; cite40†Rafailov et al., 2023 ; cite39†Chu et al., 2025 ), on representative open-source LLMs, Qwen-3 (cite41†Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.1 (cite42†Grattafiori et al., 2024 ), and conduct alignment training using widely used safety datasets (cite43†Xu et al., 2023 ; cite75†Tian et al., 2023 ; cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ; cite44†Ji et al., 2024 ; cite45†Han et al., 2024 ) (Methods, “Safety alignment”).
L203: We then compare the performance of LLMs before and after alignment on our EVIL benchmark.
L204: Our experimental results reveal limitations in existing alignment frameworks: safety alignment with these approaches on existing safety datasets not only fail to address but may also inadvertently amplify LLMs’ complicit facilitation behaviors, while their impact on responsibility and credibility remains limited (Figure cite76†13 ).
L205: Specifically, we observe that SFT consistently demonstrates a negative effect on model safety, resulting in a statistically significant decline in safety performance for Qwen-3 in the Chinese context and Llama-3.1 in both contexts (chi-squared tests, all $P<0.001$ after Bonferroni correction for three comparisons). DPO yields marginally superior safety outcomes compared to SFT (e.g., modest safety improvements on Qwen-3), yet it still fails to achieve consistent reductions in complicit behaviors.
L206: With respect to responsibility and credibility, neither SFT nor DPO provides substantial improvements on Qwen-3 and may even have significant adverse effects (e.g., SFT in both contexts and DPO in the US context, all yielding $\Delta<0$; $P<0.001$ after chi-squared tests and Bonferroni correction).
L207: As for Llama-3.1, although SFT and DPO raise the responsibility rates in both jurisdictions and the credibility rates in the Chinese context, its baseline performance on these metrics is extremely low—the responsibility and credibility rates in the Chinese context are 0.70% and 0.11%, respectively, and 1.10% and 3.44% in the US context. Consequently, even after alignment, both rates remain well below 60% and 10%, respectively.
L208: These findings indicate that current mainstream safety alignment approaches and datasets remain insufficient for effectively mitigating LLMs’ complicit facilitation of illicit instructions, and may in fact, exacerbate such behaviors. This underscores the urgent need for future research to develop safety training frameworks that can effectively mitigate LLMs’ complicit behaviors in scenarios involving legal risks.
L209: ## Discussion
L210: The first finding of this study is that widely deployed LLMs consistently exhibit complicit facilitation—providing support or guidance that enables unlawful activities—when responding to illicit instructions. While prior safety evaluations have touched upon how LLMs handle illegal requests (cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ; cite9†Zhang et al., 2024 ), these studies significantly underestimate actual risks.
L211: For example, GPT-4 achieves over 90% safety rates in both Chinese and English tests of the “Illegal Activity” category in SafetyBench (cite9†Zhang et al., 2024 ). Such results may have fostered a false sense of safety about model behavior in high-risk legal contexts. In contrast, our study uncovers widespread complicit facilitation behaviors exhibited by LLMs across both Chinese and US legal contexts, with the majority of models providing safe responses for less than 75% illicit instructions in both contexts.
L212: Notably, GPT-4o, one of the most widely deployed models globally, provides substantive assistance to nearly half of the illicit instructions in our benchmark.
L213: Furthermore, we observe substantial variation in the safety performance of LLMs across a wide range of socio-legal contexts, including differences in illicit scenarios and intents, as well as disparities across user demographic identities.

L351: ### Safety alignment
L352: To investigate whether current safety alignment strategies can effectively mitigate the complicit facilitation phenomenon observed in LLMs, we implement two widely used safety alignment techniques—supervised fine-tuning (SFT) (cite38†Wei et al., 2021 ) and direct preference optimization (DPO) (cite40†Rafailov et al., 2023 )—on two representative open-source LLMs: Qwen-3 (cite41†Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.1 (cite42†Grattafiori et al., 2024 ).
L353: These models are aligned using existing widely used safety datasets (Chinese context: CValues (cite43†Xu et al., 2023 ; cite75†Tian et al., 2023 ), SafetyPrompts (cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ); US context: PKU-SafeRLHF (cite44†Ji et al., 2024 ), WildGuardMix (cite45†Han et al., 2024 )).
L354: Consistent with common practices in LLM alignment research (cite118†Zhang et al., 2023 ; cite39†Chu et al., 2025 ; cite119†He et al., 2025 ), we fine-tune the models on a mixture of safety-specific and general-purpose (UltraFeedback-Chinese for the Chinese context and UltraFeedback-binarized for US (cite120†Cui et al., 2023 )) datasets. Following alignment, we evaluate the resulting model variants on illicit instructions from EVIL.
L355: Details on model implementation and training are provided in the Supplementary Information (“Safety alignment experiments”).
L356: ### Statistics information
L357: 
L358: In the safety assessment, each model response is assigned a binary safety label: 1 for safe, and 0 for unsafe (i.e., complicit facilitation). Within each analysis dimension (e.g., scenario type, intent category, or user identity), responses are aggregated as binomial counts—number of safe responses (successes) over total responses (trials). Group-level safety performance is measured by the safety rate, defined as the proportion of safe responses.
L359: Categorical comparisons are conducted using Pearson’s chi-squared ($\chi^{2}$) tests on contingency tables; all tests are two-sided. For $2\times 2$ tables, Yates’s continuity correction is applied. As all expected cell counts exceed five, Fisher’s exact test is not used. We report risk differences (absolute difference in safety rates) with 95% confidence intervals.
L360: These analyses support comparisons across scenario types (e.g., personal vs property-related vs societal, and violent vs non-violent), illicit intent categories (e.g., subjective factors vs objective factors, facilitation vs deceptive justification), and user demographic groups (e.g., pairwise comparisons by gender, age, race/ethnicity, and religion; multi-group comparisons by occupation).
L361: Associations involving continuous predictors are examined using logistic regression. In Study 3, we analyze the relation between occupational prestige and safety, and separately model safety rates as a function of group-level stereotype scores (warmth, competence, and their interaction). Heteroscedasticity-consistent HC3 standard errors are computed, and we report coefficient estimates, 95% confidence intervals, and $P$ values. Model fit is evaluated using Cox-Snell pseudo-$R^{2}$.
L362: All statistical tests are two-sided with a significance threshold of $0.05$. For multiple comparisons within a defined family of tests (e.g., age-based comparisons), Bonferroni correction is applied. Violin plots with box-whisker overlays display medians and interquartile ranges; error bars denote 95% confidence intervals for safety rates. Analyses are performed in Python using SciPy for contingency tests and statsmodels for regression modeling.
L363: ### Data availability
L364: 
L365: All datasets used in this study are publicly available. Illicit instruction construction for the Chinese legal context draws on publicly available court judgments from cite93†China Judgments Online (2013) , while for the US legal context, we use court judgment data released by the cite94†Caselaw Access Project (2024) . The EVIL benchmark constructed in this study is available at cite121†https://huggingface.co/datasets/TsinghuaNLP/EVIL†huggingface.co .

L779: For competence, we examine the association between occupational prestige and model-perceived competence across occupational groups (Supplementary Fig. cite229†10 ). L781: ### Safety alignment experiments
L782: We conduct all experiments with LLaMA-Factory, an open-source framework that provides unified pipelines for LLM fine-tuning (cite230†Zheng et al., 2024 ). Full-parameter updates are performed using eight A800 GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 (cite231†Rasley et al., 2020 ) in bfloat16 precision. We fine-tune Qwen3-8B (cite41†Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.1-8B (cite42†Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) with the maximum sequence length set to 1,800 tokens.
L783: We use learning rates of $1\times 10^{-5}$ for SFT and $5\times 10^{-7}$ for DPO. Optimization follows a cosine learning rate schedule with a 10% warmup. For DPO, we use a sigmoid preference loss with $\beta=0.1$. During training, we evaluate after every 500 steps on a 1% held-out validation split to monitor training stability. Final results are evaluated using the model checkpoints obtained after training for two epochs.
